look_here_first: Start with the broad, loose, cloudlike PANICLE on a basal clump. Follow individual long, spreading, flexible branches and note the small spikelets spaced apart. A mature head can detach and tumble. Purple color is only a supporting cue, not the ID; compare panicle BRANCHING and spikelet clustering with E. secundiflora.

project_inclusion.range_basis: Hays, Gillespie, and Kerr — specimen-backed county records in Hagenbuch & Lemke. Burnet — UT Plant Resources Center Burnet County treatment.

best_field_traits: leaf blades broader than E. lugens, often 3–7 mm wide
conspicuous tuft of hairs at top of sheath
panicle very open and broadly spreading

spikelets widely spaced rather than densely clumped
inflorescence often purple to reddish-purple and tumbleweed-like at maturity
morphology_keys.comparison_training: E. spectabilis is the broad airy purple one. E. secundiflora has denser clustered spikelets and ascending branches; E. lugens has much narrower involute foliage and a less flamboyant panicle.
morphology_keys.field_teaching_note: Panicle can detach as a whole at maturity; this is supportive but not unique. Kew/GrassBase gives mature spikelets often 5–7 mm long, 7–11 florets; compare intact mature material, not a field photo alone.
morphology_keys.crew_recognition_summary: BROAD OPEN TUMBLING CLOUD with individual spikelets spaced along fine spreading branches; purple is optional.

Side-on mature panicle branch to show widely spaced separate spikelets.
Spikelet macro with calipers; sheath/collar in late-season plants.

comparisons.key_distinctions: E. secundiflora: comparatively chunky panicle, much larger many-flowered spikelets clumped along shorter ascending branches. E. intermedia and E. trichodes: also airy; sheath-throat and mature spikelet details needed. Witchgrass (Panicum capillare) may resemble a fine cloud but has different reproductive spikelet structure.

field_photo_quickcheck.heading: Eragrostis spectabilis — follow the real-photo field cues
steps: START with three locally hosted exact-species photographs: the broad open panicle and thin divergent branchlets are field-recognition clues, not diagnostic spikelet anatomy.
AT ONE LOWER PANICLE BRANCH AXIL, look for a tuft of long hairs: the Burnet County anatomical treatment reports branch-node hairs about 2–4 mm. The broad-view arrows do not currently prove the hairs.

OPEN THE TRUE LEAF COLLAR: the ligule is a minute short-ciliate membrane about 0.2–0.4 mm; separate it from the conspicuous longer sheath-apex hairs (~2–4 mm). Photograph both in focus with a 1-mm ruler, not a guessed ligule arrow.

A MATURE SPIKELET should be around 4–7 mm long and about 1–2.5 mm wide, with multiple awnless florets; the Burnet County description gives lemmas about 1.5–2.3 mm and two persistent unequal glumes. Inspect isolated organs under 10–20×.

COMPARE red lovegrass E. secundiflora: clustered larger spikelets on shorter branches versus widely spaced smaller spikelets on fine branchlets here. For E. intermedia and E. trichodes confirm the true sheath/ligule and counted spikelets before species-level certainty.
Teach seasonal form: purple color varies or disappears when dry, and mature panicles may detach and tumble; color and detached tumbleweed silhouettes are not stand-alone IDs.
field_photo_quickcheck.field_rule: Wide transparent open panicle + spaced small many-flowered awnless spikelets + extremely short ciliate ligule set apart from 2–4 mm sheath-apex hairs; confirm fine anatomy at scale.
field_photo_quickcheck.warning: All 3 gallery images physically local and the comparison panel labeled as other species. Only gross-structure arrows currently justified; no licensed true-collar or isolated-scale spikelet closeup added in this pass. Minnesota Wildflowers morphology macro and university photo sources are reference-only without established image redistribution permissions. Added one CC BY-SA 4.0 lower-tuft image showing REAL basal blades (not exposed ligule); true collar/spikelet/glume/lemma photos remain essential.

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 01 · LOOK HERE FIRST
field_id_short_tiles.short: A broad, airy panicle with small separated spikelets
field_id_short_tiles.details: Follow a whole flowering stem to its widely spreading, fine, often slightly stiff panicle branches. Kew describes an open panicle approximately 25–45 cm long and 15–30 cm wide. Spikelets are carried separately on slender stalks, not bunched into dense groups. Fresh purple is a helpful memory cue but turns tan and is never decisive alone.
field_id_short_tiles.status: REAL GROSS FLOWERING STRUCTURES PRESENT; SAME-PLANT SCALE GAP

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 02 · FIND THE PERENNIAL CROWN
field_id_short_tiles.short: Short knotty rhizomes and mostly basal leaves
field_id_short_tiles.details: A warm-season perennial tuft with short knotty rhizomes, usually roughly 40–75 cm culms and 3–7 mm blades in Kew's treatment. Mature flowering panicles may break away as tumbleweeds; a loose dried head without its original crown cannot prove growth form. Current gallery photos show flowering clumps, but not a continuous locally vouchered crown-to-spikelet sequence.
field_id_short_tiles.status: PUBLISHED GROWTH FORM; NEEDS_PUBLIC_PHOTO — CONNECTED ROOTED CROWN

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 03 · COUNT FLORETS AND MEASURE GLUMES
field_id_short_tiles.short: Usually 5–7 mm spikelets, 7–11 florets in Kew
field_id_short_tiles.details: Under a 10–20× lens, measure an intact laterally compressed spikelet: Kew gives about 5–7 mm by 1.5–2 mm and 7–11 fertile florets; broader regional accounts include about 3–7.5 mm and 4–12 florets. Two short basal one-veined glumes are roughly 1–2.3 mm in Go Botany. These figures come from botanical treatments, not measured pixels in the current three photos.
field_id_short_tiles.status: NEEDS_PUBLIC_PHOTO — CALIBRATED MATURE SPIKELET AND TWO GLUMES

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 04 · CHECK THE LEMMA, PALEA AND AWNS
field_id_short_tiles.short: Three-veined, roughly 1.4–2.5 mm lemmas; no long awns
field_id_short_tiles.details: Separate one mature floret. Regional descriptions give three-veined fertile lemmas about 1.4–2.5 mm and paleas around 1–2.4 mm; the florets have no projecting awns. Photograph the actual lemma dorsal veins, palea and floret attachment beside a millimeter scale. Do not place a glume or lemma arrow on the existing wide panicle photographs.

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 05 · OPEN THE COLLAR, NOT A STEM NODE
field_id_short_tiles.short: Very short true ligule region beside longer sheath-throat hairs
field_id_short_tiles.details: Inspect the blade–sheath junction at 10–30×. Kew describes the ligule as a FRINGE OF HAIRS; regional keys may describe a minute ciliate membranous base (~0.2–0.4 mm), while conspicuous oral/sheath-throat hairs can be several millimeters long. Do not measure those long sheath hairs as the tiny membrane. Document both separately with a 1-mm scale; published descriptions differ in how the hair fringe and membrane are characterized.
field_id_short_tiles.status: NEEDS_PUBLIC_PHOTO — ACTUAL LIGULE BASE VS ORAL HAIRS

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 06 · SEPARATE RED LOVEGRASS AND WITCHGRASS
field_id_short_tiles.short: Widely spaced many-flowered spikelets, not clustered or one-flowered
field_id_short_tiles.details: E. secundiflora tends to have denser groups of larger spikelets on shorter ascending branches; E. intermedia and E. trichodes can also be airy and require sheath and mature spikelet checks. Panicum capillare and Digitaria cognata can make a tumbleweed-like cloud but have fundamentally different spikelet/floret architecture. The existing E. secundiflora panel is explicitly DIFFERENT SPECIES; verify same-angle local photographs before a finished comparison.
field_id_short_tiles.status: LOOK-ALIKE LESSON; NEEDS_PUBLIC_PHOTO — MATCHED LOCAL COMPARISON

grass_species_finalization_20261024.scientific_caution: Kew treats ligule as hair fringe; other descriptions measure a tiny ciliate membrane and separately long sheath-throat hairs. Do not identify or arrow an exact membrane from wide photos. Published 5–7 mm Kew spikelets overlap broader 3–7.5 mm regional variation.
NEEDS_PUBLIC_PHOTO: One locally verified rooted flowering E. spectabilis specimen with short knotty rhizome, crown, leaves and attached whole open panicle against cm ruler.
Opened true blade–sheath collar at 10–30× with 1-mm scale showing minute ligule base and separately longer sheath-throat/oral hairs; add arrows only after pixel inspection.
Same-specimen open panicle branch axil with documented hairs and millimeter ruler.
Three ripe 3–7.5 mm multi-flowered spikelets with both short basal glumes separately visible, floret count and actual 1-mm scale.
Dissected 3-veined awnless lemma and palea on scale; matched same-angle E. secundiflora and E. intermedia/trichodes comparison if available.
NEEDS_SITE_QA: Preserve and check three physically archived exact-species JPEGs and all original Public Domain/CC BY-SA 4.0 credits; preserve other-species E. secundiflora comparison attribution.
Inspect all existing gross arrows against original pixels and phone display; do not add microscopic glume/ligule labels to wide images.
Confirm actual rights-filtered public species gallery, attribution and photo-index order in a successful Pages deployment; GitHub JSON commit alone is not deployment.
Mark FINISHED only after measured local diagnostic anatomy, credible look-alike comparison and public photo/arrow QA pass.
